# Panel Data: Comparing a Unit with Itself {#panel-data}

```{r setup-11, include = FALSE}
source("_common.R")
library(ggplot2)
```

Every regression so far has used a cross-section: many units, each observed
once. A worker, a household, a district, a firm — one row each.

Unit \@ref(multiple-regression) tried to make such comparisons fair by measuring
the other differences between units and holding them constant. It could do that
only for what we measured. The farmer's skill, the quality of the soil, the
honesty of the district administration, the management culture of the firm — the
differences most likely to matter are exactly the ones that never appear in a
survey.

Now suppose each unit is observed **more than once**. The same farms, season
after season. The same states, year after year. The same households, revisited.

That changes what is possible. A farm observed twice can be compared **with
itself**. Whatever about the farm stays the same between the two visits — its
soil, its location, its owner's temperament — cancels out of the comparison,
whether or not anyone ever measured it.

This unit is about how to use that idea properly. We spend most of our time on
one estimator, the **fixed effects estimator**, because understanding what it
does — and what it quietly throws away — is the heart of panel data analysis.
Two others follow: **random effects**, which is more efficient when its
assumption holds, and **correlated random effects**, which sits between them and
turns out to be the most useful of the three.

## The same unit, observed again {#pd-motivation}

::: {.question}
Does fertiliser raise yield — or do farms with good soil simply use more of it?
:::

Suppose we want to know how much fertiliser raises crop yield. A survey of 1,000
farms in a single season records yield and fertiliser use, and the two are
strongly positively related.

Is that the effect of fertiliser?

Not necessarily. Farms with better soil get higher yields whatever they do, and
they may also find fertiliser more worthwhile, so they use more of it. Soil
quality is then driving both numbers. The cross-section cannot separate the two
stories, and soil quality is not in the survey to control for.

Recall the thought experiment of Section \@ref(sr-motivation): the same student,
observed twice, differing only in attendance. A cross-section can never supply
it, because no unit appears twice. A panel can supply something close to it.

Follow one farm through five seasons. Its soil does not change. If its yield
rises in the seasons it applies more fertiliser, the soil cannot be the
explanation, because the soil was the same in all five seasons. The comparison
is between the farm and itself.

::: {.keyidea}
**Panel data** follow the same units over several time periods. Their value is
that a unit can be compared with itself, which removes every characteristic that
stays fixed over time — measured or not.
:::

## What panel data look like {#pd-structure}

Panel data are usually stored in **long form**: one row for each unit in each
period.

To learn how the methods behave we need to know the truth, so we begin with a
simulated panel in which we do. This is the same device Unit \@ref(interval-estimation)
used for confidence intervals: build a world, run the method, and compare with
what we built.

```{r pd-make}
make_panel <- function(N = 200, T = 5, beta = 0.30, rho = 0.6, gamma = 0.20,
                       seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  a     <- rnorm(N, sd = 0.5)            # soil quality: never observed
  habit <- rnorm(N, sd = 0.5)            # a farm's lasting fertiliser habit
  canal <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.4)             # on a canal: fixed, observed
  d <- data.frame(farm = rep(1:N, each = T), season = rep(1:T, times = N))
  d$canal  <- canal[d$farm]
  d$lfert  <- 1 + rho * a[d$farm] + habit[d$farm] + rnorm(N * T, sd = 0.5)
  d$lyield <- 2 + beta * d$lfert + gamma * d$canal + a[d$farm] +
              rnorm(N * T, sd = 0.3)
  d$soil   <- a[d$farm]                  # kept only so we can check our work
  d
}

farms <- make_panel(seed = 11)
head(farms[, c("farm", "season", "lfert", "lyield", "canal")], 10)
```

There are `r length(unique(farms$farm))` farms observed over
`r length(unique(farms$season))` seasons, so `r nrow(farms)` rows. `lfert` is the
log of fertiliser applied and `lyield` the log of yield. A panel in which every
unit appears in every period is **balanced**; otherwise it is
**unbalanced**.

The truth is built in. Each extra 1% of fertiliser raises yield by **0.30%**: the
true $\beta_1$ is 0.30. Soil quality `soil` ($a_i$) also raises yield, and farms
with better soil use more fertiliser (`rho = 0.6`). The column `soil` is kept
only so that we can check our answers; a real survey would not have it.

### The model {-}

Write the outcome for unit $i$ in period $t$ as

$$y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{it} + a_i + u_{it},
\qquad i = 1,\ldots,N, \quad t = 1,\ldots,T$$

There are two kinds of unobserved influence here, and keeping them apart is the
whole subject.

::: {.keyidea}
- $a_i$ is the **unobserved effect**: everything about unit $i$ that is
  constant over time and not in the model. It has no $t$ subscript.
- $u_{it}$ is the **idiosyncratic error**: whatever changes from period to
  period. A good season, a pest outbreak, a delayed delivery of seed.

Their sum, $v_{it} = a_i + u_{it}$, is the **composite error**. Pooled OLS treats
$v_{it}$ as a single error term.
:::

### Two sources of variation {-}

Any variable in a panel varies in two ways: **between** units (farm 7 uses more
fertiliser than farm 8, on average) and **within** a unit over time (farm 7 used
more this season than last). The decomposition is exact.

```{r pd-variation}
demean <- function(v, g) v - ave(v, g)          # subtract each unit's own mean

within_sd  <- function(v, g) sd(demean(v, g))
between_sd <- function(v, g) sd(tapply(v, g, mean))

round(rbind(
  lfert  = c(overall = sd(farms$lfert),
             between = between_sd(farms$lfert, farms$farm),
             within  = within_sd(farms$lfert, farms$farm)),
  lyield = c(overall = sd(farms$lyield),
             between = between_sd(farms$lyield, farms$farm),
             within  = within_sd(farms$lyield, farms$farm))), 3)
```

Fertiliser use differs a good deal between farms and less within a farm over
time. This matters because, as we are about to see, the fixed effects estimator
uses **only the within column**.

## Why pooling fails {#pd-pooled}

::: {.question}
What goes wrong if we ignore the panel structure and run OLS on all
`r nrow(farms)` rows?
:::

**Pooled OLS** stacks every observation and regresses $y$ on $x$ as if each row
were an independent draw.

```{r pd-pooled}
pooled <- lm(lyield ~ lfert, data = farms)
round(coef(summary(pooled)), 4)
```

The estimate is `r round(coef(pooled)[2], 3)`, against a truth of 0.30. Two
different things have gone wrong.

### Problem 1: bias {-}

The soil quality $a_i$ sits inside the composite error $v_{it}$. If it is
correlated with fertiliser use, pooled OLS violates the zero conditional mean
assumption exactly as in Section \@ref(mlr-causal): the omitted variable bias
formula applies, with $a_i$ as the omitted variable.

$$\text{plim}\,\hat{\beta}_1^{\text{pooled}} = \beta_1 +
\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x_{it}, a_i)}{\mathrm{Var}(x_{it})}$$

We can check this against the simulation, which tells us every ingredient.

```{r pd-bias-formula}
cov_xa <- 0.6 * 0.5^2                    # rho times Var(a)
var_x  <- 0.6^2 * 0.5^2 + 0.5^2 + 0.5^2 # soil + habit + season-to-season noise
round(c(truth = 0.30, bias = cov_xa / var_x,
        predicted = 0.30 + cov_xa / var_x,
        pooled_estimate = unname(coef(pooled)[2])), 3)
```

The estimate is far above the truth, and close to what the formula predicts (this
is one sample; the average over many panels, in Section \@ref(pd-mc), is 0.555).
It would be mistaken to call this a small-sample accident: a bigger panel would
only estimate the wrong number more precisely.

### Problem 2: standard errors {-}

The second problem is separate, and it would remain even if there were no bias.
The same $a_i$ appears in all five of a farm's composite errors, so those errors
are **correlated with one another**. Pooled OLS assumes they are independent.

```{r pd-icc}
farms$res_pooled <- resid(pooled)
wide <- reshape(farms[, c("farm", "season", "res_pooled")],
                idvar = "farm", timevar = "season", direction = "wide")
round(cor(wide[, -1])[1:3, 1:3], 2)
```

Residuals from the same farm in different seasons correlate at about 0.7.
Treating `r nrow(farms)` rows as `r nrow(farms)` independent pieces of
information overstates how much we know, and the usual standard errors are too
small — the same lesson as Section \@ref(ols-hetero), for a different reason.

The remedy is the **cluster-robust standard error**, which allows arbitrary
correlation among the observations of one unit and treats the unit, not the
row, as the independent draw.

```{r pd-cluster-fn}
cluster_se <- function(m, cluster) {
  X <- model.matrix(m); u <- residuals(m); G <- length(unique(cluster))
  bread <- solve(crossprod(X))
  meat  <- crossprod(rowsum(X * u, cluster))   # sum scores within each unit
  sqrt(diag(G / (G - 1) * bread %*% meat %*% bread))
}

round(c(usual = coef(summary(pooled))[2, 2],
        clustered = cluster_se(pooled, farms$farm)[2]), 4)
```

The clustered standard error is about 50% larger. Cluster at the level of the
unit that is observed repeatedly, and use these standard errors for every
estimator in this unit.

Clustering repairs only problem 2. It does nothing for problem 1: an estimate
that is centred on the wrong number is no better for having an honest
standard error.

### Seeing it {-}

Plot twelve farms. Each farm has its own cloud of five points, and its own
trend within the cloud.

```{r pd-lines, fig.height = 4.6}
set.seed(21)
pick <- sample(unique(farms$farm), 12)
sub  <- farms[farms$farm %in% pick, ]

ggplot(sub, aes(lfert, lyield, colour = factor(farm), group = farm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(pooled)[1], slope = coef(pooled)[2],
              colour = book_palette$ink, linewidth = 1.3, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Log fertiliser", y = "Log yield",
       title = "Each farm's own slope is shallow; the pooled line is steep",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: pooled OLS. Coloured lines: each farm on its own") +
  theme_book()
```

Within any one farm the relationship is flat-ish — about 0.30. Across farms the
clouds are stacked: farms to the right sit higher, because they have better
soil. The dashed pooled line mixes the two, so it is far steeper than any single
farm's own line. The fixed effects estimator is an average of the farms' *own*
lines.

## The fixed effects estimator {#pd-fe}

::: {.question}
What exactly does the fixed effects estimator do — and what does it throw away?
:::

### The within transformation {-}

Start with the model for one unit, and **average it over time**:

$$\bar{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{x}_i + a_i + \bar{u}_i,
\qquad \text{where } \bar{y}_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} y_{it}$$

Because $a_i$ does not change with $t$, it appears in the averaged equation
exactly as it appeared in the original. Now **subtract** the averaged equation
from the original, period by period:

::: {.theory}
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{it} - \bar{y}_i
  &= \beta_1 (x_{it} - \bar{x}_i) + (a_i - a_i) + (u_{it} - \bar{u}_i)
  \\[4pt]
\ddot{y}_{it} &= \beta_1 \ddot{x}_{it} + \ddot{u}_{it}
\end{aligned}
$$

where a double dot marks a variable **minus its unit's own time average**. The
intercept $\beta_0$ cancels too, and so does $a_i$.
:::

This is the **fixed effects transformation**, also called the **within
transformation**. The unobserved effect has vanished from the equation. Whatever
$a_i$ is, and however it is related to $x$, it cannot bias an estimate made from
this equation because it is no longer there.

The **fixed effects (within) estimator** is OLS on the transformed variables:

$$\hat{\beta}_1^{FE} = \frac{\sum_{i}\sum_{t} \ddot{x}_{it}\,\ddot{y}_{it}}
                          {\sum_{i}\sum_{t} \ddot{x}_{it}^{\,2}}$$

Nothing about it is exotic. It is the slope formula of Unit \@ref(ols), applied
to deviations from each unit's own mean instead of deviations from the overall
mean.

```{r pd-fe-demean}
farms$y_dd <- demean(farms$lyield, farms$farm)
farms$x_dd <- demean(farms$lfert,  farms$farm)

fe_by_hand <- sum(farms$x_dd * farms$y_dd) / sum(farms$x_dd^2)
c(fixed_effects = fe_by_hand, pooled = unname(coef(pooled)[2]), truth = 0.30)
```

The fixed effects estimate is `r round(fe_by_hand, 3)`, close to the truth, where
pooled OLS gave `r round(coef(pooled)[2], 3)`.

::: {.intuition}
A farm with good soil has high $y$ in all five seasons and high $x$ in all five.
Subtracting the farm's own averages shifts the whole cloud of that farm's points
to the origin, wherever it started. Good soil and bad soil are now the same
cloud. All that survives is how the farm moves around *its own centre*: a season
with more fertiliser than usual against a season with less.

The comparison is the one we wanted: each farm against itself.
:::

The identifying assumption is **strict exogeneity**: given $a_i$, the
idiosyncratic error in *every* period is uncorrelated with the explanatory
variable in *every* period. What the estimator does **not** require is that
$a_i$ be uncorrelated with $x$. It permits arbitrary correlation between the
unobserved effect and the explanatory variables, in every period. That is its
whole advantage.

### The same number, three ways {-}

The fixed effects estimate can be reached by several routes. They agree exactly.

**Route 1: the demeaned regression** is the one above.

**Route 2: dummy variables.** Treat each farm's $a_i$ as a parameter to be
estimated — a separate intercept for each farm — by including a dummy for every
farm, exactly as in Unit \@ref(dummy-variables).

$$y_{it} = \beta_1 x_{it} + \underbrace{\alpha_1 D1_i + \alpha_2 D2_i + \cdots + \alpha_N DN_i}_{\text{one intercept per farm}} + u_{it}$$

```{r pd-lsdv}
lsdv <- lm(lyield ~ lfert + factor(farm), data = farms)

c(demeaned = fe_by_hand, dummies = unname(coef(lsdv)["lfert"]))
length(coef(lsdv))
```

The coefficient on `lfert` is identical to every digit. It is the
**dummy variable regression**, or LSDV (least squares dummy variables). With 200
farms the model has `r length(coef(lsdv))` parameters. That is why nobody runs it
in a large panel: the demeaning route gives the same slope without ever
estimating the 200 intercepts.

The agreement is Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (Section \@ref(mlr-fwl)) at work. Including
a dummy for every farm and then asking for the effect of $x$ is the same as
first removing from $x$ and $y$ the part explained by the farm dummies — and
what is left after regressing a variable on a full set of unit dummies is
precisely its deviation from the unit mean.

**Route 3: first differences.** Subtract the previous period instead of the unit
mean:

$$\Delta y_{it} = y_{it} - y_{i,t-1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Delta y_{it} = \beta_1 \Delta x_{it} + \Delta u_{it}$$

$a_i$ cancels here too. With two periods this is the same estimator again. The
next sections return to when the two differ.

::: {.watchout}
All three routes remove $a_i$ by comparing a unit only with itself, so all three
are **blind to anything constant over time** and all three use only within-unit
variation. Their differences are in efficiency and in what they assume about
$u_{it}$, not in what they can see.
:::

### The degrees of freedom {-}

The demeaned regression is an ordinary OLS regression on $NT$ rows with one
slope, so one might expect $NT - 1$ degrees of freedom, and a standard error
computed accordingly. That is wrong.

Within each farm, the demeaned errors $\ddot{u}_{it}$ must add up to zero,
because they are deviations from the farm's own average. They are therefore not
$T$ free numbers but $T - 1$. Each of the $N$ units costs one degree of freedom,
and the correct count is

$$\text{df} = NT - N - k = N(T-1) - k$$

where $k$ is the number of slopes. An `lm()` on demeaned data does not know this
and uses $NT - k$.

```{r pd-df}
n <- nrow(farms); N <- 200; k <- 1
m_dd <- lm(y_dd ~ x_dd - 1, data = farms)

s2_naive     <- sum(resid(m_dd)^2) / (n - k)
s2_corrected <- sum(resid(m_dd)^2) / (n - N - k)

round(c(
  se_from_lm_on_demeaned = coef(summary(m_dd))[1, 2],
  se_correct_df          = sqrt(s2_corrected / sum(farms$x_dd^2)),
  se_from_dummy_regression = coef(summary(lsdv))["lfert", 2]), 5)
```

The dummy-variable regression gets the degrees of freedom right automatically,
since it knows it estimated 200 intercepts. A package's fixed effects routine
corrects for it as well. The correction matters most when $T$ is small: here it
raises the standard error by about 12%, and with $T = 2$ the naive standard error
would be too small by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

### The fit {-}

Two $R^2$ figures can be reported, and they answer different questions.

```{r pd-r2}
r2_within <- summary(m_dd)$r.squared
r2_lsdv   <- summary(lsdv)$r.squared
round(c(within = r2_within, with_dummies = r2_lsdv), 3)
```

The **within $R^2$** is the share of the *time variation* in $y$ explained by the
time variation in $x$ — the fit of the demeaned equation. The $R^2$ of the dummy
regression is far higher, because 200 farm dummies explain most of the
variation between farms. That high number is not an achievement. It says that
farms differ a lot, which we knew, and tells us nothing about how well
fertiliser explains yield.

### The farm intercepts {-}

The unobserved effects themselves can be recovered, because $a_i$ is the part of
the farm's average yield that its average fertiliser does not explain:

$$\hat{\alpha}_i = \bar{y}_i - \hat{\beta}_1^{FE}\,\bar{x}_i$$

(These are the dummy coefficients of the LSDV regression. Packages that report an
overall "intercept" after fixed effects usually report the average of the
$\hat{\alpha}_i$.)

```{r pd-ahat}
ybar <- tapply(farms$lyield, farms$farm, mean)
xbar <- tapply(farms$lfert,  farms$farm, mean)
ahat <- ybar - fe_by_hand * xbar

truth <- tapply(2 + 0.20 * farms$canal + farms$soil, farms$farm, mean)

round(c(correlation_with_truth = cor(ahat, truth)), 3)
```

The estimated intercepts track the true ones closely, but only closely. Each is
based on just $T = 5$ observations, and unlike $\hat{\beta}_1$ they do **not**
become reliable as we add farms: a new farm brings a new $a_i$ to be estimated,
so no information about any one $a_i$ accumulates. Only a longer $T$ would help.
That is why we treat $a_i$ as something to be removed, not as something to be
estimated.

### What the transformation throws away {-}

Subtracting a unit's average removes $a_i$, but it removes **anything else that
is constant over time** with it. `canal` — whether the farm lies on a canal — is
observed, but it never changes for a given farm, so

$$\ddot{canal}_{it} = canal_i - canal_i = 0 \quad \text{for every } i \text{ and } t$$

```{r pd-timeinv}
farms$canal_dd <- demean(farms$canal, farms$farm)
range(farms$canal_dd)

coef(lm(y_dd ~ x_dd + canal_dd - 1, data = farms))
```

The coefficient on `canal` is `NA`: R reports that the variable is a column of
zeros and cannot be estimated. In the dummy regression the same thing is
visible as perfect collinearity, because `canal` equals a combination of farm
dummies.

::: {.watchout}
**The fixed effects estimator cannot estimate the effect of any variable that is
constant over time.** Gender, caste, a farm's location, years of schooling in a
panel of adults, a state's colonial history, distance to a river: all are swept
away along with $a_i$. This is the price of the estimator's main virtue. It
cannot be paid back by a larger sample.
:::

Two partial escapes are worth knowing.

First, a time-constant variable can be **interacted with year dummies**. Years
of schooling cannot enter, but "schooling × 2019" and "schooling × 2020" can,
and their coefficients show how the return to schooling *in each year differs from
the return in the base year*. Neither the base-year return nor any year's
return can be recovered, only the changes.

Second, the **correlated random effects** approach later in this unit can
estimate a coefficient on a time-constant variable while still allowing $a_i$ to
be correlated with the time-varying regressors — under a stronger assumption
about the time-constant variable.

A related trap: if you include a full set of year dummies, you cannot estimate
the effect of a variable whose change over time is the same for everyone.
Experience in a panel of workers who are all employed in every year rises by
exactly one every year. Its within variation is identical to a time trend, and
a time trend is exactly what year dummies capture.

```{r pd-exper}
farms$experience <- farms$season + 5      # every farm gains one season a year

with_years <- lm(lyield ~ lfert + factor(season) + experience + factor(farm),
                 data = farms)
coef(with_years)["experience"]
```

Again `NA`. The farm effect absorbs how much experience a farm began with; after
that, experience cannot be told apart from the season dummies.

### Fixed effects or first differences? {-}

Both estimators remove $a_i$. When do they differ?

**With two periods they are the same estimator**, provided each is run properly:
the first-difference regression needs an intercept (the change in the average
outcome between the two periods), which in the fixed effects version appears as
a dummy for the second period.

```{r pd-fd-t2}
two <- subset(farms, season <= 2)
two <- two[order(two$farm, two$season), ]

dy <- two$lyield[two$season == 2] - two$lyield[two$season == 1]
dx <- two$lfert [two$season == 2] - two$lfert [two$season == 1]

fd_t2 <- coef(lm(dy ~ dx))["dx"]
fe_t2 <- coef(lm(lyield ~ lfert + factor(season) + factor(farm),
                 data = two))["lfert"]
round(c(first_difference = unname(fd_t2), fixed_effects = unname(fe_t2)), 6)
```

**With three or more periods they differ**, although both are consistent as $N$
grows. The choice turns on the idiosyncratic errors $u_{it}$.

```{r pd-fd-t5}
farms <- farms[order(farms$farm, farms$season), ]
first_diff <- function(v, g) ave(v, g, FUN = function(z) c(NA, diff(z)))
farms$dy <- first_diff(farms$lyield, farms$farm)
farms$dx <- first_diff(farms$lfert,  farms$farm)

fd_t5 <- coef(lm(dy ~ dx - 1, data = farms))["dx"]
round(c(first_difference = unname(fd_t5), fixed_effects = fe_by_hand), 4)
```

- If the $u_{it}$ are **serially uncorrelated** — a bad season now says nothing
  about the next — fixed effects is the more efficient estimator, and its standard
  errors are the ones to believe. This is the usual maintained assumption.
- If the $u_{it}$ are **highly persistent**, so that shocks accumulate like a
  random walk, then the *differences* $\Delta u_{it}$ are uncorrelated and first
  differencing is better.
- Nothing about the demeaned residuals tells you which holds, because they are
  not the $u_{it}$. A test is available in the differenced equation.

When the two estimators give very different answers it is worth reporting both
and asking why.

### Fixed effects and measurement error {-}

The fixed effects estimator pays a price for working only with within variation.
If $x$ is measured with error, the damage depends on how much of the true
variation survives. Fertiliser use is recorded from memory; suppose each
recorded value carries an error with standard deviation 0.4.

```{r pd-measerr, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(3)
one_rep <- function() {
  d <- make_panel()
  d$lfert_noisy <- d$lfert + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.4)
  fe_slope <- function(x) {
    xd <- demean(x, d$farm); yd <- demean(d$lyield, d$farm)
    sum(xd * yd) / sum(xd^2)
  }
  c(clean = fe_slope(d$lfert), noisy = fe_slope(d$lfert_noisy))
}
rowMeans(replicate(300, one_rep()))
```

A noise standard deviation of 0.4 is a modest part of the *overall* variation in
fertiliser (standard deviation about 0.8). But a large part of that overall
variation is *between* farms, which fixed effects discards. What remains —
the within variation — is smaller, so the same noise is a larger share of it
and attenuates the slope more. The estimate falls from 0.30 to about 0.18.

::: {.watchout}
Removing the unobserved effect by differencing out the between variation makes
the problem of **classical measurement error worse**, not better. Panel methods
that remove bias from one source can amplify it from another. If $x$ is noisy
and mostly persistent, a fixed effects estimate may be biased towards zero.
:::

### Unbalanced panels and attrition {-}

Real panels often have gaps: some units are missing in some periods. Fixed
effects handles this without difficulty. Each unit's mean is taken over **its
own** periods, one degree of freedom is lost per unit, and the rest is unchanged.

```{r pd-unbal}
unbal <- farms[!(farms$farm %in% 1:10 & farms$season > 1), ]   # 10 farms seen once
table(Periods_observed = table(unbal$farm))
```

A unit observed only **once** plays no role at all. Its demeaned $x$ and $y$ are
exactly zero. In this panel ten farms contribute nothing to the fixed effects
estimate, although they remain in the data.

The harder question is *why* the panel is unbalanced. Suppose farms disappear
from the survey.

- If a farm drops out for reasons related to $a_i$ — farms on poor soil are more
  likely to be lost to follow-up — fixed effects is **still fine**, because $a_i$
  is removed from the estimating equation anyway. This is a real advantage over
  methods that need $a_i$ to be uncorrelated with everything.
- If the farm drops out for reasons related to the **idiosyncratic error**
  $u_{it}$ — farms are lost precisely because a bad season ruined them — the
  remaining sample is selected on the outcome, and the estimates are biased.

### Inference {-}

Fixed effects standard errors assume $u_{it}$ is homoskedastic and serially
uncorrelated. Neither is safe to assume, and both are easy to relax by
clustering on the unit, exactly as for pooled OLS.

```{r pd-fe-se}
c(classical = coef(summary(lsdv))["lfert", 2],
  clustered = cluster_se(lsdv, farms$farm)["lfert"])
```

Cluster whenever the unit is observed repeatedly. With few units — say, fewer
than about twenty states — cluster-robust standard errors themselves become
unreliable, and a long $T$ with small $N$ raises further difficulties not
discussed here.

### What to remember about fixed effects {-}

::: {.keyidea}
- The estimator **demeans** each unit's data and runs OLS: the unobserved effect
  $a_i$ and every other time-constant variable disappear.
- It permits **any** correlation between $a_i$ and the explanatory variables. It
  needs *strict exogeneity* of the time-varying errors.
- It is identical to OLS with a dummy for each unit; the demeaned version just
  avoids estimating the dummies. Degrees of freedom are $N(T-1) - k$.
- It uses **only within variation**. Units that never vary, and variables that
  never vary, contribute nothing.
- With $T = 2$ it equals first differencing; with $T \ge 3$ the two differ, and
  fixed effects is preferred when $u_{it}$ is not highly persistent.
- It is **not** a cure for omitted variables that *change* over time, and it
  can aggravate measurement error.
:::

### The between estimator {-}

For completeness, the opposite operation: regress unit **averages** on unit
averages and use only between variation.

$$\bar{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{x}_i + (a_i + \bar{u}_i)$$

```{r pd-between}
unit <- data.frame(ybar = as.numeric(ybar), xbar = as.numeric(xbar))
between <- coef(lm(ybar ~ xbar, data = unit))["xbar"]
round(c(between = unname(between), within = fe_by_hand, truth = 0.30), 3)
```

The between estimate is far from the truth, because $a_i$ is correlated with
$\bar{x}_i$. If $a_i$ is related to $x$, the between estimator is biased. It is
mainly useful as a building block, as the next sections show.

## Random effects {#pd-re}

::: {.question}
What if we are willing to assume that the unobserved effect is *not* correlated
with the explanatory variables?
:::

Fixed effects pays for its robustness by discarding the between variation. If
$a_i$ were uncorrelated with $x_{it}$ — if soil quality had nothing to do with
how much fertiliser a farm uses — pooled OLS would not be biased, and the between
variation would be perfectly good information about $\beta_1$. Discarding it
would waste data.

The **random effects** model makes that assumption. It treats $a_i$ as a random
draw from a population, independent of the regressors:

$$\mathrm{Cov}(x_{it}, a_i) = 0 \quad \text{for all } t$$

Under this assumption pooled OLS is consistent — but still inefficient and with
wrong standard errors, since the composite error is serially correlated:

$$\mathrm{Var}(v_{it}) = \sigma_a^2 + \sigma_u^2, \qquad
\mathrm{Corr}(v_{it}, v_{is}) = \frac{\sigma_a^2}{\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_u^2}
\quad (t \neq s)$$

The efficient way to estimate a regression with an error of this known structure
is **generalised least squares**. For this error structure GLS has a particularly
simple form: it is OLS after subtracting only *part* of each unit's mean.

::: {.theory}
Define the **quasi-demeaned** variables

$$y_{it} - \theta\,\bar{y}_i, \qquad x_{it} - \theta\,\bar{x}_i,
\qquad \theta = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + T\sigma_a^2}}$$

Running OLS on these variables, including an intercept (which is multiplied by
$1-\theta$), gives the random effects estimator.
:::

Look at the two extremes of $\theta$.

- $\theta = 0$: nothing is subtracted, and random effects is **pooled OLS**. This
  happens when $\sigma_a^2 = 0$: there is no unobserved effect to worry about.
- $\theta = 1$: the whole unit mean is subtracted, and random effects is the
  **fixed effects** estimator. This happens as $T$ or $\sigma_a^2$ gets large.

Random effects is therefore a weighted compromise between the within estimator
and the between estimator. Where is it on the scale?

```{r pd-theta, fig.height = 3.8}
th <- expand.grid(T = 2:30, ratio = c(0.25, 1, 4))
th$theta <- 1 - sqrt(1 / (1 + th$T * th$ratio))
th$ratio <- factor(th$ratio, labels = c("sigma_a^2 / sigma_u^2 = 0.25",
                                        "= 1", "= 4"))

ggplot(th, aes(T, theta, colour = ratio)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(book_palette$soft, book_palette$accent,
                                 book_palette$reject), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Number of periods T", y = expression(theta),
       title = "Random effects moves towards fixed effects as T grows",
       subtitle = "At θ = 1 it is fixed effects; at θ = 0 it is pooled OLS") +
  theme_book() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The more periods we have, and the bigger the unobserved effect relative to the
idiosyncratic noise, the more random effects behaves like fixed effects.

In practice $\sigma_a^2$ and $\sigma_u^2$ must themselves be estimated. A simple
approach (Swamy–Arora) uses the residual variance from the within regression for
$\sigma_u^2$, and the between regression to back out $\sigma_a^2$.

```{r pd-re-fn}
# Fixed and random effects for one regressor, balanced panel.
fe_re <- function(d, id, y, x) {
  g <- d[[id]]; n <- nrow(d); N <- length(unique(g)); T <- n / N
  yb <- ave(d[[y]], g); xb <- ave(d[[x]], g)
  yd <- d[[y]] - yb;    xd <- d[[x]] - xb

  b_fe  <- sum(xd * yd) / sum(xd^2)
  s2u   <- sum((yd - b_fe * xd)^2) / (n - N - 1)
  se_fe <- sqrt(s2u / sum(xd^2))

  btw   <- lm(yb ~ xb, data = data.frame(yb, xb)[!duplicated(g), ])
  s2a   <- max(sum(resid(btw)^2) / (N - 2) - s2u / T, 0)
  theta <- 1 - sqrt(s2u / (s2u + T * s2a))

  yq <- d[[y]] - theta * yb; xq <- d[[x]] - theta * xb
  re <- lm(yq ~ I(rep(1 - theta, n)) + xq - 1)
  c(b_fe = b_fe, se_fe = se_fe,
    b_re = unname(coef(re)[2]), se_re = coef(summary(re))[2, 2],
    theta = theta, sigma2_a = s2a, sigma2_u = s2u)
}

est <- fe_re(farms, "farm", "lyield", "lfert")
round(est, 4)
```

The estimated variance components are reasonably close to the truth
($\sigma_a^2 = 0.25$, $\sigma_u^2 = 0.09$), and `theta` is `r round(est["theta"], 2)`: random effects subtracts about
`r round(100 * est["theta"])`% of each farm's mean.

Look at the slope. The random effects estimate is
`r round(est["b_re"], 3)`: higher than the fixed effects estimate of
`r round(est["b_fe"], 3)`, and higher than the truth of 0.30. It is not
as wrong as pooled OLS, because it removes part of the farm effect, but it is
still biased — because soil is correlated with fertiliser, and random effects
assumes it is not.

::: {.watchout}
**Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects only if its assumption is
true.** If $\mathrm{Cov}(x_{it}, a_i) \neq 0$ it is inconsistent, and a large
sample only makes the wrong answer more precise. Fixed effects makes no such
assumption.
:::

## Fixed or random? The Hausman test {#pd-hausman}

::: {.question}
Can the data tell us whether the random effects assumption holds?
:::

Compare the two estimators. If $a_i$ is uncorrelated with $x$, both are
consistent and should give similar answers. If it is correlated, fixed effects
is still consistent and random effects is not, and they should differ.

This is the logic of the **Hausman test**. Under $H_0$ (random effects valid) the
two estimators estimate the same number, and the random effects one is efficient:

$$H = \frac{\big(\hat{\beta}^{FE} - \hat{\beta}^{RE}\big)^2}
           {\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\beta}^{FE}) - \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\beta}^{RE})}
\;\sim\; \chi^2_1 \quad \text{(for one slope)}$$

A large $H$ rejects $H_0$: the estimators disagree by more than sampling noise
would allow, and fixed effects should be preferred.

```{r pd-hausman}
hausman <- function(e) {
  h <- (e["b_fe"] - e["b_re"])^2 / (e["se_fe"]^2 - e["se_re"]^2)
  c(H = unname(h), p_value = unname(1 - pchisq(h, 1)))
}
round(hausman(est), 5)
```

The test rejects emphatically here, as it should, since we built the data to
violate the random effects assumption.

::: {.watchout}
The Hausman test has three limitations.

1. The variance formula assumes random effects is efficient, which requires the
   errors to be homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated apart from $a_i$. With
   clustering, the denominator can come out **negative**, and the test is invalid.
2. It compares slopes only. It says nothing about whether the fixed effects
   estimate is *right* — only that the two differ.
3. A failure to reject is not proof that random effects is valid; in small panels
   the test has little power.
:::

The next section gives a version of the test that does not rely on any of these.

## Correlated random effects {#pd-cre}

::: {.question}
Is there a way to keep the fixed effects estimate, test the random effects
assumption, and still estimate the effect of `canal`?
:::

The **correlated random effects** (CRE) approach, due to Mundlak and
Chamberlain, makes the same reasoning that underlies fixed effects explicit.

The random effects problem is that $a_i$ may be related to $x_{it}$. So model
that relationship directly. Suppose $a_i$ depends on the farm's *average*
fertiliser use:

$$a_i = \psi\,\bar{x}_i + c_i, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(x_{it}, c_i) = 0$$

Here $c_i$ is whatever is left of the unobserved effect after the part related
to $\bar{x}_i$ has been taken out. It **is** uncorrelated with $x$, by
construction. Substitute into the model:

$$y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{it} + \psi\,\bar{x}_i + c_i + u_{it}$$

This is a random effects model with one extra regressor: the **unit mean of
$x$**. The problem that made random effects biased has been moved into an
explicit, estimated term.

```{r pd-cre}
farms$xbar <- ave(farms$lfert, farms$farm)

cre <- lm(lyield ~ lfert + xbar, data = farms)

round(rbind(
  coef(summary(cre))[c("lfert", "xbar"), 1:2],
  fixed_effects = c(fe_by_hand, NA)), 4)
```

Three results follow from adding $\bar{x}_i$.

::: {.keyidea}
1. **The coefficient on $x_{it}$ equals the fixed effects estimate** — here
   `r round(coef(cre)["lfert"], 4)`, to every digit. Controlling for the unit's
   average makes the remaining variation in $x$ the *within* variation, so the
   coefficient measures the same thing as the within estimator.
2. **The coefficient on $\bar{x}_i$ is the difference between the between and
   the within effects**: $\hat{\psi} = \hat{\beta}^{B} - \hat{\beta}^{W}$.
   A farm using more fertiliser *on average* has a higher yield for reasons
   that go beyond what extra fertiliser does within a farm.
3. **Testing $\psi = 0$ is a test of the random effects assumption.** If $\psi =
   0$, the between and within effects coincide and random effects is valid. It is
   the Hausman test in regression form.
:::

Checking point 2 against the between estimate computed earlier:

```{r pd-cre-between}
round(c(psi_hat = unname(coef(cre)["xbar"]),
        between_minus_within = unname(between) - fe_by_hand), 4)
```

Point 3 has a considerable practical advantage over the Hausman test: the
regression can use **cluster-robust standard errors**, so the test remains valid
when the errors are heteroskedastic or serially correlated.

```{r pd-cre-test}
se_cre <- cluster_se(cre, farms$farm)
t_psi  <- coef(cre)["xbar"] / se_cre["xbar"]
round(c(psi_hat = unname(coef(cre)["xbar"]),
        clustered_se = unname(se_cre["xbar"]),
        t_statistic = unname(t_psi)), 3)
```

$t$ is very large, so $\psi \neq 0$ and the random effects assumption is
rejected — the same message as the Hausman test, now in a form that survives
clustering.

### Recovering time-constant variables {-}

The key practical gain: once $\bar{x}_i$ is in the equation, time-constant
variables such as `canal` can be added, and their coefficients **are** estimable.

```{r pd-cre-canal}
cre2 <- lm(lyield ~ lfert + canal + xbar, data = farms)
round(cbind(estimate = coef(cre2),
            clustered_se = cluster_se(cre2, farms$farm))[2:4, ], 4)
```

The estimated effect of `canal` is `r round(coef(cre2)["canal"], 3)` (standard
error about 0.06), against a true value of 0.20, with the fixed effects estimator
unable to produce any number at all. The slope on `lfert` is unchanged.

::: {.watchout}
This is not free. The coefficient on `canal` is credible only if `canal` is
uncorrelated with $c_i$, the part of the unobserved effect left over after
$\bar{x}_i$ is accounted for. In the simulation we made it so — `canal` is
independent of soil. In a real panel that is a substantive assumption about the
time-constant variable, and it is stronger than anything fixed effects needed.
The time-varying coefficient $\hat{\beta}_1$ does **not** depend on it.
:::

::: {.deeper}
With several time-varying regressors, include the unit mean of **each**:
$\bar{x}_{1i}, \bar{x}_{2i}, \ldots$. With an **unbalanced** panel the means are
taken over each unit's own available periods.

Chamberlain's more general version replaces the single mean by the entire
history, $x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{iT}$, which allows $a_i$ to depend on the *pattern*
of $x$ over time rather than just its average. Mundlak's version is much easier
to use and usually all that is needed.

Adding the means to a pooled OLS regression with clustered standard errors gives
the same coefficients as above, in a balanced panel; it is the random-effects
weighting that would, in general, differ.
:::

## All four on trial {#pd-mc}

::: {.question}
Do these four estimators really behave as claimed?
:::

We have one sample of 200 farms. To see how each estimator behaves in general,
simulate many panels and record each estimate. We do it twice: once with soil
correlated with fertiliser (as before) and once with `rho = 0`, so that the
random effects assumption is true.

```{r pd-mc, cache = TRUE}
four_estimates <- function(d) {
  e <- fe_re(d, "farm", "lyield", "lfert")
  xb <- ave(d$lfert, d$farm)
  c(Pooled = unname(coef(lm(lyield ~ lfert, data = d))["lfert"]),
    Fixed   = unname(e["b_fe"]),
    Random  = unname(e["b_re"]),
    CRE     = unname(coef(lm(lyield ~ lfert + xb, data = d))["lfert"]))
}

set.seed(2026)
run_mc <- function(rho, reps = 600)
  t(replicate(reps, four_estimates(make_panel(rho = rho))))

mc <- rbind(
  data.frame(run_mc(0.6), world = "Soil correlated with fertiliser"),
  data.frame(run_mc(0.0), world = "Soil uncorrelated with fertiliser"))

methods <- c("Pooled", "Fixed", "Random", "CRE")
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, function(m)
  data.frame(world = mc$world, method = m, estimate = mc[[m]])))
long$method <- factor(long$method, levels = methods)

ggplot(long, aes(method, estimate, fill = method)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.size = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.30, colour = book_palette$reject, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(book_palette$soft, book_palette$accent,
                               book_palette$fill, book_palette$ink)) +
  facet_wrap(~ world) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimated effect of fertiliser",
       title = "600 panels, true effect 0.30 (horizontal line)") +
  theme_book()
```

```{r pd-mc-table}
summ <- function(d) round(rbind(mean = colMeans(d[, 1:4]),
                                sd   = apply(d[, 1:4], 2, sd)), 3)
list(correlated   = summ(mc[mc$world == "Soil correlated with fertiliser", ]),
     uncorrelated = summ(mc[mc$world == "Soil uncorrelated with fertiliser", ]))
```

The pattern is the whole content of this unit.

- **Soil correlated with fertiliser.** Pooled and random effects are biased;
  fixed effects and CRE are centred on 0.30.
- **Soil uncorrelated with fertiliser.** All four are unbiased. Random effects
  is the most precise; fixed effects and CRE give up a little precision by
  ignoring the between variation, and pooled OLS is the *least* precise of
  all, because it ignores the serial correlation.

CRE gets the consistency of fixed effects for the time-varying coefficient.
What it does not do is make fixed effects any *more efficient* — its slope has
the same spread. Its extra value is the test of $\psi = 0$ and the ability to
include time-constant variables.

## Real data: profit and scale in Indian states {#pd-asi}

::: {.question}
Do industrial profits rise with the size of a state's manufacturing sector?
:::

The file `asi-state-profit.csv` has the gross value added (GVA) and profit of
registered manufacturing in each state, by year, taken from the Annual Survey of
Industries. We ask whether, in a year when a state's manufacturing sector is
larger, a larger fraction of its value added is retained as profit.

The outcome is the **profit share** (profit divided by GVA), the explanatory
variable the log of GVA. We keep the 21 states observed in all 43 years from
1980 to 2023 so that the panel is balanced.

```{r pd-asi-data}
asi <- read.csv("data/asi-state-profit.csv")
years_seen <- table(asi$state)
asi <- asi[asi$state %in% names(years_seen)[years_seen == 43], ]
asi$lgva <- log(asi$gva)
asi$xbar <- ave(asi$lgva, asi$state)

c(states = length(unique(asi$state)), rows = nrow(asi))
```

Profit share is bounded above by 1 and can be strongly negative in bad years,
so a few extreme values will matter.

```{r pd-asi-fit}
pooled_a <- lm(profit_share ~ lgva, data = asi)
fe_a     <- lm(profit_share ~ lgva + factor(state), data = asi)
cre_a    <- lm(profit_share ~ lgva + xbar, data = asi)
est_a    <- fe_re(asi, "state", "profit_share", "lgva")

res <- rbind(
  Pooled = c(coef(pooled_a)["lgva"], cluster_se(pooled_a, asi$state)["lgva"]),
  Fixed  = c(coef(fe_a)["lgva"],     cluster_se(fe_a, asi$state)["lgva"]),
  Random = c(est_a["b_re"], NA),
  CRE    = c(coef(cre_a)["lgva"],    cluster_se(cre_a, asi$state)["lgva"]))
colnames(res) <- c("Estimate", "Clustered SE")
round(res, 4)
```

The pooled slope is `r round(coef(pooled_a)["lgva"], 3)`; fixed effects is
`r round(coef(fe_a)["lgva"], 3)`. A state where manufacturing is larger than
*its own* usual level retains about 0.8 percentage points more of value added as
profit for each 10% rise in GVA ($0.083 \times 0.10$). Pooled OLS understates it,
since it also compares states that differ in size for other reasons.

Now test whether the random effects assumption holds.

```{r pd-asi-test}
round(hausman(est_a), 4)

se_psi <- cluster_se(cre_a, asi$state)["xbar"]
round(c(psi_hat = unname(coef(cre_a)["xbar"]), clustered_se = unname(se_psi),
        t = unname(coef(cre_a)["xbar"] / se_psi)), 3)
```

The Hausman test is borderline ($p$ close to 0.06) and the clustered test on
$\hat{\psi}$ does not reject. Different questions, different answers, and here
neither is decisive. With only 21 states, no test is going to be definitive.

### Time matters too {-}

Everything so far removed what is constant over time within a state. But
profit shares, GVA and prices all drift over 43 years for reasons that affect
every state at once: inflation, liberalisation, a changing mix of industries.
Anything common to all states in a year can be absorbed by adding a **dummy for
each year** — the unit-and-time version of fixed effects, called **two-way fixed
effects**.

```{r pd-asi-twoway}
fe2_a  <- lm(profit_share ~ lgva + factor(state) + factor(yr), data = asi)
cre2_a <- lm(profit_share ~ lgva + xbar + factor(yr), data = asi)

round(rbind(
  `Fixed, state only`    = c(coef(fe_a)["lgva"],  cluster_se(fe_a, asi$state)["lgva"]),
  `Fixed, state + year`  = c(coef(fe2_a)["lgva"], cluster_se(fe2_a, asi$state)["lgva"]),
  `CRE: coefficient on x` = c(coef(cre2_a)["lgva"], cluster_se(cre2_a, asi$state)["lgva"]),
  `CRE: coefficient on mean` = c(coef(cre2_a)["xbar"], cluster_se(cre2_a, asi$state)["xbar"])),
  4)
```

The estimate **more than doubles**, to `r round(coef(fe2_a)["lgva"], 3)`, once
year effects are included. GVA is measured in current rupees, so it rises in
every state every year with inflation, and the profit share has its own trend; a
regression that ignores common time effects mixes that trend into the slope.
After removing it, a state's own deviation from its yearly norm is what
remains. And now the CRE coefficient on the mean is different from zero
($t \approx -2.4$), so the random effects assumption fails once time is
controlled for.

::: {.watchout}
The two sets of results are a reminder that a specification choice can change the
answer as much as the choice of estimator. Neither state nor year dummies will
remove a **time-varying, state-specific** influence — a state's policy change in
1995, a new industrial estate — and a causal reading of 0.18 would need an
argument that no such influence moves with GVA. Fixed effects supports the
claim "within a state, in years when GVA is high, the profit share is high".
It does not by itself support "raising GVA raises profits".
:::

## Choosing and using the estimators {#pd-choosing}

| Question | If **yes** | If **no** |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Could $a_i$ be correlated with the regressors? | Fixed effects or CRE | Random effects is possible |
| Do you need the effect of a time-constant variable? | CRE (with an assumption) | Fixed effects |
| Is there a trend or shock common to all units? | Add time dummies | — |
| Is $T$ very small and $N$ large? | Cluster on the unit | Take extra care with inference |

Some practical principles.

1. **Default to fixed effects** (or CRE) when the question is causal. The
   random effects assumption — that the unobserved effect is unrelated to
   everything in the model — is rarely credible for the questions economists ask.
2. **Report the Mundlak test, not only the Hausman test**, because it survives
   clustering.
3. **Fixed effects removes only what is constant over time.** An omitted
   variable that changes within the unit, in a way related to $x$, still biases
   the estimate.
4. **Cluster standard errors on the unit.** Always.
5. **Check how much within variation there is.** If $x$ barely changes within
   units, the fixed effects estimate will be imprecise, and measurement error
   will be a larger share of what does vary.
6. **Do not interpret the unit dummies.** They are controls, not findings.

::: {.deeper}
When the regressors include a **lagged dependent variable**, $y_{i,t-1}$, strict
exogeneity fails by construction, and fixed effects is biased. The bias shrinks
at rate $1/T$ (the "Nickell bias"), so it is small in a long panel and large in a
short one. The usual remedies are instrumental-variable estimators in
differences. They go beyond this book, but you should know to be suspicious of
any short-panel regression with a lagged outcome on the right-hand side.
:::

## Summary {#pd-summary}

::: {.keyidea}
- **Panel data** follow the same units over several periods. A unit can then be
  compared with itself, which removes everything about it that stays constant.
- The model is $y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{it} + a_i + u_{it}$. $a_i$ is the
  **unobserved effect**, constant over time; $u_{it}$ is the **idiosyncratic
  error**; their sum is the **composite error**.
- **Pooled OLS** is biased when $a_i$ is correlated with $x$, and its standard
  errors are wrong because the composite errors of one unit are correlated.
  Cluster-robust standard errors fix only the second problem.
- The **fixed effects (within) estimator** subtracts each unit's time average
  from every variable, so $a_i$ drops out, and runs OLS. It permits arbitrary
  correlation between $a_i$ and $x$. Degrees of freedom are $N(T-1) - k$.
- It is **identical** to OLS with a dummy for every unit, and with $T = 2$ it is
  identical to first differencing.
- It uses **only within variation**, so it cannot estimate the effect of any
  variable constant over time, and it can worsen measurement error.
- A unit observed once contributes nothing. **Attrition** related to $a_i$ is
  harmless; attrition related to $u_{it}$ is not.
- **Random effects** assumes $\mathrm{Cov}(x_{it}, a_i) = 0$ and estimates by GLS,
  subtracting a fraction $\theta$ of each unit's mean. It lies between pooled OLS
  ($\theta = 0$) and fixed effects ($\theta = 1$), and is the most efficient
  estimator **only if** its assumption holds.
- The **Hausman test** compares fixed and random effects. It is invalid under
  clustering and heteroskedasticity.
- **Correlated random effects** adds the unit means of $x$ to the regression.
  The coefficient on $x$ equals the fixed effects estimate, the coefficient on
  the mean tests the random effects assumption robustly, and time-constant
  variables become estimable — under a stronger assumption about them.
- In the simulation, pooled and random effects were biased (about 0.55 and 0.35
  against 0.30) when soil was related to fertiliser; fixed effects and CRE were
  not.
:::

## Practice problems {#pd-practice}

::: {.yourturn}
Work each one before opening the solution. The
[question bank](#pd-question-bank) that follows has no answers.
:::

### Numerical problems {-}

**11.1** Three farms are each observed in three seasons. $x$ is fertiliser and
$y$ is yield.

| Farm | $x_{i1}$ | $x_{i2}$ | $x_{i3}$ | $y_{i1}$ | $y_{i2}$ | $y_{i3}$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 7 |
| 2 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 10 | 10 |
| 3 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 5 | 9 | 10 |

i. Compute each farm's mean of $x$ and of $y$.
ii. Compute the demeaned values $\ddot{x}_{it}$ and $\ddot{y}_{it}$.
iii. Compute the fixed effects estimate $\hat{\beta}_1$.
iv. Is the pooled OLS slope larger or smaller than your answer? Why?

::: {.answer}
```{r pd-ex1, echo = FALSE}
x <- c(1,2,3, 4,5,6, 2,4,6); y <- c(2,3,7, 7,10,10, 5,9,10)
f <- rep(1:3, each = 3)
```

**(i)** $\bar{x} = 2, 5, 4$ and $\bar{y} = 4, 9, 8$ for farms 1, 2, 3.

**(ii)** Farm 1: $\ddot{x} = (-1, 0, 1)$, $\ddot{y} = (-2, -1, 3)$. Farm 2:
$\ddot{x} = (-1, 0, 1)$, $\ddot{y} = (-2, 1, 1)$. Farm 3:
$\ddot{x} = (-2, 0, 2)$, $\ddot{y} = (-3, 1, 2)$.

**(iii)** $\sum\ddot{x}\ddot{y} = (2+0+3) + (2+0+1) + (6+0+4) = 18$ and
$\sum\ddot{x}^2 = 2 + 2 + 8 = 12$, so $\hat{\beta}_1^{FE} = 18/12 = 1.5$.

**(iv)** The pooled slope is `r round(coef(lm(y ~ x))[2], 3)`, larger than 1.5.
Farms with higher $x$ also have higher average $y$, in a way the within-farm
movements do not account for: farm 2 has both the largest $x$ and the largest
$y$ on average. Pooled OLS credits all of that to $x$, which is the same
composite-error bias as in the simulation. Check: `lm(y ~ x + factor(f))`
reproduces 1.5.
:::

**11.2** A panel has $N = 50$ units and $T = 6$ periods. A fixed effects model is
estimated by running OLS on demeaned data with three regressors, and the
software reports a standard error of 0.040 for one coefficient.

i. How many degrees of freedom did the regression use, and how many should it
   have used?
ii. By what factor should the reported standard error be multiplied?
iii. Give the corrected standard error.

::: {.answer}
**(i)** It used $NT - k = 300 - 3 = 297$. The correct figure is
$NT - N - k = 300 - 50 - 3 = 247$.

**(ii)** The estimate of $\sigma_u^2$ is a sum of squared residuals divided by
the degrees of freedom, so the standard error scales with
$\sqrt{297/247} = `r round(sqrt(297/247), 4)`$.

**(iii)** $0.040 \times `r round(sqrt(297/247), 4)` =
`r round(0.040 * sqrt(297/247), 4)`$.
:::

**11.3** A researcher estimates a log-wage equation on a panel of workers with
fixed effects. For each variable, say whether its coefficient can be estimated,
and why.

i. Union membership, which changes for some workers.
ii. Gender.
iii. Years of schooling, in a panel of adults whose schooling is complete.
iv. Years of work experience, with a full set of year dummies, where every worker
    is employed in every year.
v. Years of schooling interacted with the year dummies.

::: {.answer}
**(i)** Yes: it varies within workers.

**(ii)** No. It is constant for each worker, so it is removed by the within
transformation.

**(iii)** No, for the same reason: constant for each adult.

**(iv)** No. Experience rises by one for every worker every year, so after the
worker's effect is removed it is perfectly collinear with the year dummies.

**(v)** Yes, but only the *differences* in the return to schooling between each
year and the base year. The return in any single year is not identified.
:::

**11.4** Estimated variance components in a random effects model are
$\hat{\sigma}_a^2 = 0.04$ and $\hat{\sigma}_u^2 = 0.16$.

i. Compute $\theta$ for $T = 4$.
ii. Compute $\theta$ for $T = 16$.
iii. What does the difference tell you about how random effects relates to fixed
     effects as $T$ grows?
iv. Compute the correlation between two composite errors from the same unit.

::: {.answer}
**(i)** $\theta = 1 - \sqrt{0.16/(0.16 + 4 \times 0.04)} = 1 - \sqrt{0.5} =
`r round(1 - sqrt(0.5), 3)`$.

**(ii)** $\theta = 1 - \sqrt{0.16/(0.16 + 16 \times 0.04)} = 1 - \sqrt{0.2} =
`r round(1 - sqrt(0.2), 3)`$.

**(iii)** $\theta$ rises with $T$: random effects subtracts more of each unit's
mean and moves towards fixed effects ($\theta = 1$).

**(iv)** $0.04/(0.04 + 0.16) = 0.2$.
:::

**11.5** Fixed and random effects estimates of one slope are
$\hat{\beta}^{FE} = 0.30$ with standard error 0.040, and $\hat{\beta}^{RE} =
0.35$ with standard error 0.030.

i. Compute the Hausman statistic.
ii. The 5% critical value of $\chi^2_1$ is 3.84. What do you conclude?
iii. Why would you not be reassured if a colleague reported the result of this
     test from a regression with clustered standard errors?

::: {.answer}
**(i)** $H = (0.30 - 0.35)^2/(0.040^2 - 0.030^2) = 0.0025/0.0007 =
`r round(0.0025/0.0007, 3)`$.

**(ii)** It is below 3.84, so we do not reject the random effects assumption at
5% ($p \approx `r round(1 - pchisq(0.0025/0.0007, 1), 3)`$). It is close to the
boundary, so the conclusion is fragile.

**(iii)** The formula takes the difference of the two variances, which is
justified only if random effects is efficient. With clustered standard errors
that is no longer true, and the denominator can be negative or meaningless. The
regression form of the test, adding the unit means, avoids the problem.
:::

**11.6** A CRE regression of log wage on union status (time-varying) and its
unit mean gives the following, with clustered standard errors.

| | Estimate | SE |
|:--|--:|--:|
| union | 0.08 | 0.02 |
| mean of union | 0.14 | 0.05 |

i. What is the fixed effects estimate of the union effect?
ii. What is the between effect of union status?
iii. Test whether random effects is valid, and state the conclusion.

::: {.answer}
**(i)** 0.08. In a CRE regression the coefficient on the time-varying variable
equals the fixed effects estimate.

**(ii)** The coefficient on the mean is the between effect minus the within
effect, so the between effect is $0.14 + 0.08 = 0.22$.

**(iii)** $t = 0.14/0.05 = 2.8$, which exceeds 1.96. Reject $\psi = 0$: the
unobserved effect is related to the unit's average union status, and random
effects would be biased. Workers who are more often unionised earn more than
the within-worker change in union status can explain, probably because of
unobserved differences between workers.
:::

**11.7** In a pooled regression, $\mathrm{Var}(x) = 0.40$ and
$\mathrm{Cov}(x, a) = 0.12$. The true $\beta_1 = 0.50$.

i. What does pooled OLS estimate in a large sample?
ii. What would it estimate if $\mathrm{Cov}(x, a) = 0$?
iii. What does fixed effects estimate in the first case?

::: {.answer}
**(i)** $0.50 + 0.12/0.40 = 0.80$.

**(ii)** 0.50 — the unobserved effect no longer biases it, though the standard
errors are still wrong.

**(iii)** 0.50, whatever the covariance. Fixed effects allows any correlation
between $a_i$ and $x$.
:::

**11.8** Four units are each observed in two periods.

| Unit | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $y_1$ | $y_2$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 5 |
| 3 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 11 |
| 4 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 12 |

i. Compute the first-difference slope, with an intercept.
ii. Verify that the fixed effects estimate is the same.

::: {.answer}
```{r pd-ex8, echo = FALSE}
x1 <- c(1,2,3,4); x2 <- c(2,2,5,6); y1 <- c(3,4,7,8); y2 <- c(6,5,11,12)
dx <- x2 - x1; dy <- y2 - y1
fd <- sum((dx - mean(dx)) * (dy - mean(dy))) / sum((dx - mean(dx))^2)
xx <- c(x1, x2); yy <- c(y1, y2); u <- rep(1:4, 2); tt <- rep(1:2, each = 4)
fe <- unname(coef(lm(yy ~ xx + factor(tt) + factor(u)))["xx"])
```

**(i)** $\Delta x = (1, 0, 2, 2)$, $\Delta y = (3, 1, 4, 4)$, with means 1.25 and
3. Then $\sum(\Delta x - 1.25)(\Delta y - 3) = 4.0$ and
$\sum(\Delta x - 1.25)^2 = 2.75$, so the slope is $4.0/2.75 =
`r round(4/2.75, 4)`$.

**(ii)** Fixed effects with a dummy for the second period, as the first
difference regression with an intercept requires, gives `r round(fe, 4)`. The
two are identical when $T = 2$.
:::

### R exercises {-}

**11.9** Using the simulation function of Section \@ref(pd-structure), set
`rho = 0` and `N = 100`, `T = 3`. Compute the pooled, fixed effects, random
effects and CRE estimates and the Hausman statistic. Does the Hausman test
reject? Should it?

::: {.answer}
```{r pd-ex9, eval = FALSE}
d <- make_panel(N = 100, T = 3, rho = 0, seed = 5)
e <- fe_re(d, "farm", "lyield", "lfert")
round(e, 4)
hausman(e)

xb <- ave(d$lfert, d$farm)
coef(lm(lyield ~ lfert + xb, data = d))
```

With `rho = 0` the random effects assumption is true, so the test should not
reject, and 5% of the time it will anyway — that is what a 5% significance level
means. Run it with several seeds and count the rejections.
:::

**11.10** Using `asi-state-profit.csv`, estimate the fixed effects regression of
profit share on log GVA using **all** states (the unbalanced panel), with
clustered standard errors. How many states contribute? Compare with the balanced
panel in the text.

::: {.answer}
```{r pd-ex10, eval = FALSE}
asi_all <- read.csv("data/asi-state-profit.csv")
asi_all$lgva <- log(asi_all$gva)

table(table(asi_all$state))                 # how many years each state appears

fe_all <- lm(profit_share ~ lgva + factor(state), data = asi_all)
c(coef(fe_all)["lgva"], cluster_se(fe_all, asi_all$state)["lgva"])
```

The table shows that states observed in only one year contribute nothing, since
their demeaned values are zero. Check which dropped out by counting states with
a single row. The estimate differs from the balanced-panel one because the extra
states have fewer years and a different mix of industries — and, if their
absence from the full panel is related to outcomes, because of the selection
problems discussed under unbalanced panels.
:::

**QB 11.7** In the random effects estimator, $\theta = 0$ corresponds to

a. fixed effects
b. pooled OLS
c. the between estimator
d. first differences

**QB 11.8** The coefficient on $\bar{x}_i$ in a Mundlak regression equals

b. the within effect
c. the between effect minus the within effect

## Looking ahead {#pd-looking-ahead}

Panel data buy one thing: protection against everything about a unit that stays
constant. They do not protect against what changes.

The next question follows naturally. Suppose a policy is introduced in some
states in one year and not in others. A panel of states, observed before and after,
with state and year dummies — a **two-way fixed effects** regression — compares
how outcomes changed in treated states with how they changed in untreated ones.
That comparison of changes is the idea behind **difference-in-differences**, and it
is the most widely used application of the methods in this unit.

It rests on an assumption fixed effects alone cannot test: that the treated
states, absent the policy, would have followed the same trend as the others. When
that is plausible, panel data come closest to the controlled experiment that
Section \@ref(sr-motivation) wished for.
